analysis.one_liner: Ratchets up penalties for thrift and bank fraud and gives regulators new tools to recover taxpayer losses.
analysis.headline: The bill was reported from the Senate Judiciary Committee and placed on the Senate calendar as Calendar No. 979, but it never received a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: After the savings and loan collapse, which taxpayers funded through federal deposit insurance, Senator Biden introduced this bill to crack down on bank fraud. It would have doubled maximum prison terms for bank fraud to 30 years, created a 'financial crime kingpin' offense carrying up to life imprisonment, and let regulators freeze suspects' assets before judgment. It also would have stopped convicted felons from running banks, banned golden parachute payouts at failing institutions, barred executives from using bankruptcy to escape restitution, and paid rewards to whistleblowers who report bank fraud.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who were footing the bill for the savings and loan cleanup through the deposit insurance fund and the Resolution Trust Corporation; depositors; victims of bank crimes who would get restitution and restored property; honest banks that compete against crooked ones; and whistleblowers, who would win cash awards for reporting fraud.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the maximum prison sentence for bank fraud and embezzlement from 20 to 30 years, and creates a 'continuing financial crime enterprise' offense for organized fraud rings that carries 10 years to life and fines up to $10 million per person.

Gives the FDIC, the Resolution Trust Corporation, and credit union regulators power to freeze assets through court orders so suspects cannot drain, hide, or transfer money while a fraud case is pending.
Blocks executives from using bankruptcy to wipe out restitution orders, penalties, and debts owed to regulators from breach of fiduciary duty at failed institutions.
Prohibits golden parachute payments and payouts of executives' legal liabilities at undercapitalized or failing institutions without federal approval.

Bars people convicted of bank crimes from running or controlling insured banks or credit unions, and stops convicted fraudsters who defaulted on loans from buying assets of the failed institutions they damaged.

Creates a Financial Institutions Fraud Unit inside the Justice Department, authorizes wiretaps for bank fraud, extends the time limit for prosecutions to ten years, and lets any person file confidential fraud declarations with a fund to pay informant rewards.

analysis.who_pays: Thrift and bank executives and insiders who committed or facilitated fraud, who would face far longer prison terms, forfeiture of their gains, restitution orders that survive bankruptcy, and loss of severance payouts. Taxpayers would fund modest new appropriations for prosecutors and courts.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a major expansion of federal criminal law: it raises maximum sentences to 30 years, adds a kingpin statute with life imprisonment, authorizes wiretaps for bank fraud, and allows regulators to obtain ex parte restraining orders and prejudgment attachments without posting bond, which raises due-process concerns for people only accused of wrongdoing.

New crimes like 'obstructing an examination' and broad asset-freeze powers could sweep in conduct at ordinary institutions and impose defense and compliance costs on the banking industry, including legitimate institutions caught in enforcement actions.
The bill authorizes new appropriations for the Justice Department, the federal courts, and the IRS, adding federal spending on top of the already expensive savings and loan cleanup.

Some provisions shield government discretion from judicial review, including the Attorney General's decisions on informant declarations and payments, which limits accountability for how those powers are used.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim — prosecuting the people who looted failed thrifts and recovering money for the taxpayers who insured them — addresses a real, expensive problem, and most of the tools are ones regulators asked for. The civil-liberties tradeoffs (harsh mandatory-range sentences, wiretaps, ex parte asset freezes) are real but typical of major fraud legislation. On balance a serious enforcement bill whose costs fall mostly on proven fraud, not ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee reported the bill to the Senate floor and put it on the calendar in mid-October 1990, but no vote ever came before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Biden introduced the bill on October 12, 1990 as an original measure from the Senate Judiciary Committee, which he chaired.
The committee reported it to the Senate without a written report the same day, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 979.
The bill sat on the calendar with no floor action, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 without the Senate ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executives and insiders whose thrift fraud this bill targeted — no enhanced penalties, asset-freeze powers, or bankruptcy changes took effect through this bill, and no national commission was created to examine the savings and loan failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bank fraud suspects, who faced no new penalties

for.what_they_did: Ordered the original bill reported on October 11, 1990 and reported it to the Senate without a written report the next day.

sides.party_line_note: The record contains no votes or recorded opposition; the bill simply received no floor action after being placed on the Senate calendar.

industries.industry: Thrift and bank executives and insiders
industries.note: The bill targets this group directly: longer prison terms, a kingpin statute, forfeiture, asset freezes, restitution that survives bankruptcy, bans on golden parachutes at failing institutions, and bans on convicted felons running or buying failed banks. These are the people the savings and loan cleanup was costing taxpayers hundreds of billions to cover.

All insured institutions would face new offenses (like obstructing examiners), restrictions on executive pay, and compliance costs. But stronger fraud enforcement protects the deposit insurance fund and public confidence, which benefits honest banks and their depositors.

The bill is explicitly framed as taxpayer recovery: restitution, forfeiture, and asset-recovery tools aimed at recouping losses from the savings and loan crisis, which the FDIC and Resolution Trust Corporation were absorbing with federal backing.
